To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) hearing adults who are learning sign language for the first time are able to produce entity classifiers with high accuracy, 2) hearing adults who have been learning sign language for 1-2 years are able to understand entity classifiers with high (above chance) accuracy, 3) sign-naïve individuals are able to understand sign language entity classifiers with high above-chance accuracy.
adult learners of sign language produce and comprehend classifiers with higher than random accuracy, but they do not always produce the handshapes that native signers use.

adult learners of sign language can produce entity classifiers, but they produce non-canonical handshapes, and that sign-naïve people can comprehend entity classifiers, but not as well as sign-naïve signers
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origins of sign language, and with the relationship between sign languages and gesture.
how the visuo-spatial and gestural knowledge of hearing learners of a sign language is used in the production and comprehension of classifiers.
the relationship between gesture and sign language, and with the relationship between sign languages and the visuo-spatial skills of their users.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the acquisition of sign languages is a very complicated task for the hearing learner and the use of classifiers is a very complex task for the learner of sign language.
the acquisition of sign languages is a process of conventionalization, and this process can be investigated in adult learners of sign language, who bring to the task their own gestural abilities.
the use of gesture and sign language are not mutually exclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

adult learners of sign language are more likely to produce and comprehend classifiers with the accuracy of native signers than sign-naïve controls, but that they are less likely to produce the same handshape as native signers, and that they do not show a preference to use the same handshapes as native speakers when describing the same scenes.
the acquisition process of BSL is not only influenced by the visuo-spatial abilities, but also by the gestural abilities.
the acquisition of classifiers by adult hearing learners of British Sign Language is a complex task that involves both the use and the comprehension of conventionalized handshapes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the acquisition of classifier constructions is not a straightforward matter of copying the manual gestures of native signers, but is rather a process of learning to encode visuo-spatial information with conventionalized manual gestures, and that this process can be investigated by examining the performance of hearing adult learners.
the visuo-spatial abilities of signers and non-signers are similar.
adult learners of sign language can be recruited to help us understand the relationship between gesture and sign language.
